context: factory · drawing, stranding and extrusion lines; a tall CV tower or long CCV line for MV / HV cable

brief.intro: New to this project type? A cable factory starts with copper or aluminium rod, draws it down to wire, twists (strands) the wires into a conductor, covers the conductor with insulation in an extrusion line, assembles the insulated cores together, and adds screens, armour and an outer sheath. Every finished cable is electrically tested. For low-voltage cable these are compact machines in an ordinary hall. For medium and high voltage, the insulation is applied and cured in a CV line — either a long, sloping tube (catenary) or a tower 60–150 m tall — followed by days of degassing in heated rooms and testing in a screened high-voltage laboratory. That line, its tower and the test laboratory dominate both the building and the programme.

must_get_right: Decide the voltage range first: an MV / HV plant needs a CV line with a tower or long catenary building, degassing rooms and an HV laboratory — a different project from an LV plant.
The CV tower is a tall structure with heavy equipment at the top; its construction method and crane plan belong in the schedule.
Clean conditions around the insulation extruder are essential; the clean room must be finished before the CV line is assembled.
Sales depend on type tests and utility approvals, which follow the first good production by months — include them.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by plant area along the process line and by discipline, with every long-lead machine tracked from order to factory test, shipping and arrival.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar for construction; equipment installation may run extended shifts under vendor supervision. Commissioning follows the vendor's programme, and hot commissioning runs continuously once started.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Supplier layouts → foundations and tower / catenary structure → halls and clean room → machine installation in process order → cooling water, nitrogen and power → dry runs → first cables → HV laboratory accredited → routine tests → type tests and approvals. The critical path runs through the CV line and its structure.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The process technology and vendor are fixed before design starts; vendor drawings for foundations arrive on the agreed dates; permanent power and water are available before cold commissioning; raw material for trial production is on site.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

rows: CV line (triple extrusion, curing tube, controls)

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy machines need crane access and often must enter before the cladding or a wall is closed. Vendor supervisors are booked for fixed periods. Clean, dry, powered conditions are required before precision equipment is unpacked.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: late CV line, tower construction, cleanliness problems causing test failures, late HV laboratory, and type-test failures. Contingency is held before type testing.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by plant area and discipline; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the installation crews and the vendor supervisors — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
